draft.title: Boolean algebra
card: Boolean algebra uses rules to rewrite a statement in a simpler form with the same truth value. Write ∧ for and, ∨ for or, and ¬ for not.
Laws
P ∧ P = P, P ∨ ¬P = true, P ∧ ¬P = false, and ¬(¬P) = P. De Morgan's laws: ¬(P ∧ Q) = ¬P ∨ ¬Q, and ¬(P ∨ Q) = ¬P ∧ ¬Q.
Worked example
Simplify ¬(P ∨ Q) ∨ P. De Morgan gives (¬P ∧ ¬Q) ∨ P. This is true when P is true. When P is false, ¬P is true, so it equals ¬Q. So the result is P ∨ ¬Q.
Tautology
A tautology is a statement that is true for every combination of truth values, such as P ∨ ¬P. The same laws work for sets, with union for or, intersection for and, and complement for not.
draft.remember: Use the laws to rewrite a statement more simply. A tautology is always true.

a.q: Using De Morgan's law, which statement equals ¬(P ∧ Q)?
a.why: De Morgan's law negates each part and swaps and with or, so ¬(P ∧ Q) = ¬P ∨ ¬Q. The option ¬P ∧ ¬Q is tempting, but it keeps the and, so it equals ¬(P ∨ Q).
a.clue: Negate each part and swap the connective.

b.q: Which of these statements is a tautology?
b.why: The first has the form R ∨ ¬R with R = P ∧ Q, so it is true every time. The third equals P, which is false when P is false, so it is not a tautology. The second is false when P is true, and the fourth is false when P is false and Q is true.
b.clue: Look for the form R ∨ ¬R, where R is a whole statement.

problems.detail: The why refers to options by position ('the first', 'the third'), and these do not match the order shown. It calls the tautology 'the first', but (P ∧ Q) ∨ ¬(P ∧ Q) is listed third. It says 'the third equals P', but P ∧ (Q ∨ ¬Q) is listed first. A student would be told the listed third option, which is the right answer, is not a tautology. The why should name each option by its expression, not its position.

check.summary: The card, the laws, the worked example and both answers are correct. The explanation for question b refers to options by position, and that order does not match the options shown, so it wrongly says the listed third option (the correct answer) is not a tautology.
